# Strategies for Reimagining Complex Care

J Gen Intern Med DOI: 10.1007/s11606-021-06956-6 © Society of General Internal Medicine 2021

W e applaud Epstein and Wu’s recent piece on delivering complex care for adult patients.1 Lessons learned from the sister field of pediatric complex care may be helpful for adult practitioners and researchers. While Epstein and Wu propose an outpatient intensivist model centered around primary care physicians (PCP), pediatrics has seen a rise in consultative “complex care programs,” in which academic pediatricians often lead care coordination hubs that complement community-based PCPs to support children with medical complexity (CMC).2 To ensure equitable access, many programs have adopted tele-health to support patients remotely, or tele-mentoring of rural PCPs.3 Another physician-led approach from pediatrics is the episode-based model2, in which a team of complex care experts deliver comprehensive hospital care and hospital-to-home transitions. Across pediatric models, we have learned that physicians alone cannot manage their patients’ complex health and social needs. Instead, we need local “complex care ecosystems” that engage stakeholders from physical health, behavioral health, public health, home care, and the social service sectors.4

Embracing patients and family members both as core care team members and as collaborators in national quality improvement and research efforts has been central to the pediatric complex care movement (e.g., the Collaborative Improvement and Innovation Network to Advance Care for CMC). Interdisciplinary team-based approaches could mitigate physician burnout by not placing all coordination responsibilities on a single subspecialist. We encourage exploration of how value-based payment models, including accountable care organizations and global budgets, could finance complex care. While we agree with the authors that existing physician reimbursement is insufficient for caring for complex populations, our experience in pediatrics has highlighted the need for flexible funds to invest in broad capabilities outside the physician role, such as algorithms to identify complex patients, technology platforms for care planning, and non-clinical staff to address social needs.

Pediatrics has also started to embed complex care in medical education across learner levels. Examples include the University of North Carolina’s medical student complex care elective; Stanford pediatrics residency’s complex care rotation with modules on goal-setting and care plans; and Boston Children’s Hospital two-year complex care fellowship. A recent Delphi study aimed to identify curricular priorities for caring for CMC.5 Adapting pediatric professional competencies for adult populations may be useful for internal medicine educators. In conclusion, we encourage collaboration and continued dialogue between pediatricians and internists. Leveraging lessons from serving patients across the life course can accelerate advancements in the field of complex care.
